data.name: server.instructions
data.value:
Kontext is your long-term memory, spoken in five verbs: - Retain (store something worth remembering) - Recall (search by meaning) - Reclaim (fetch by id) - Recollect (browse by type/tag) - Reinforce (say which memories you actually used)
It also indexes the database's own log, reachable two ways: - Search (find recorded events by meaning) - Query (read the log with SQL — filter, group, count)
The three answer different questions. Recall returns CLAIMS YOU WROTE — decisions, facts, open questions. Search returns RECORDS THE DATABASE HOLDS, ranked by meaning, payload included. Query answers precisely what ranking cannot: how many, since when, grouped by what. Reach for recall when you want what you concluded, search when you want the evidence underneath it, and query when the answer is a number or a list you could name in SQL.
Recall before you guess — re-deriving something you already learned is the expensive path. Retain the moment you learn something durable, written to stand on its own. STORE THE CLAIM YOU CHECKED: name what would show you wrong before storing, and if you cannot name that check, sharpen the claim until you can. Put attribution in the content — "the docs state X" is a fact you verified, a bare "X" is not. An unchecked belief is an OpenQuestion, not a weak fact. To correct a memory, retain the correction with supersedes. Reinforce what actually helped — recall refreshes everything it returns, so without you the store cannot tell a memory you used from one it merely offered. Periodically, recall broadly and retain what the pile adds up to, citing what it rests on — the synthesis is yours to do, not a tool you call.

data.name: tool.recall
data.value: Search your memory by MEANING — not reclaim (that's by id), not recollect (that's by type/tag, no ranking). Reach for this before you act on something you might already know: at the start of a task, when a name, decision, error, file, or preference comes up that you may have seen before, or any time you'd otherwise guess. Recalling is cheap; re-deriving something you already learned — or silently contradicting a past decision — is not. Results come back ranked best-first on relevance, importance and recency. There is no trust score to read: everything stored was checked when it was written, so the type tells you what KIND of claim you have, not how far to believe it. Only what is currently true surfaces — superseded memories never do. Side effect worth knowing: recalling a memory keeps it salient (refreshes its recency clock), so the things you actually use stay near the top over time. Recall freely.

data.name: tool.recall.param.options
data.value: Optional knobs — limit, minimum score, tag pre-filter, include-full. Null ⇒ server defaults.

data.name: tool.recall.param.query
data.value: What you are trying to remember, in natural language — phrase it like a question to a colleague ("what did we decide about the checkpoint format?"), not keywords.

data.name: tool.reclaim
data.value: Fetch exact memories by id — not recall (that's by meaning), not recollect (that's by type/tag). Use it for progressive disclosure: when an earlier result (a recall hit, a neighbour) handed you only ids and you now want the complete folded records, provenance (evidence, reasoning) included. Not a search and no ranking — you get exactly the ids you asked for, including superseded records (you asked by id, so they are not hidden here). Ids that don't exist are simply absent from the result, never an error — diff the returned ids against what you asked for to see which missed. Like recall, reclaiming refreshes the recency clock of the memories it returns.

data.name: tool.recollect
data.value: Browse your memories by structure, not relevance — not recall (that ranks by meaning), not reclaim (that's by id). Use it to enumerate or gather a filtered set — "every OpenQuestion in this repo", "everything I retained this week" — where you want a list, not a ranked answer to a question. Enumerating OpenQuestions at the start of a task is the canonical use: it is your work queue, and because recollect does not rank, nothing hides one from that path. The types filter is any-of (empty = any type); all supplied tags must be present. Ordered by sort (default: newest-retained first); reverse with direction. Read-only.

data.name: tool.reinforce
data.value:
Say which memories you ACTUALLY USED. Retrieval is not use: recall hands you a page and refreshes every memory on it, because the server cannot see which one you acted on — that guess is generous, and this is how you correct it. Reach for it when a memory changed your answer: it settled a question, saved you a re-derivation, or stopped you contradicting a past decision. Not for everything a recall returned, and not for something you merely read — naming everything says nothing.
REINFORCING CHANGES HOW EASILY A MEMORY IS FOUND, NEVER HOW TRUE IT IS. It is not a vote of confidence and it does not make a claim stronger; memories carry no trust score, and a reinforced OpenQuestion is still an open question. To assert something is wrong or better known now, retain a correction with supersedes.
EVERY ID MUST NAME A LIVE MEMORY, and the whole call is rejected if one does not. An id that names nothing is a bug in the caller — you got these from a recall or a reclaim. A SUPERSEDED id is worse: recall never surfaces one, so its recency clock feeds no ranking and accepting it would report success for a write nothing can ever read. It also means you acted on a claim that has since been corrected, so the rejection hands back the id that superseded it — read that one, and reinforce it instead if it is what you should have used. Writes only the recency clock; nothing is created or destroyed.

data.name: tool.reinforce.param.ids
data.value: The memories that actually informed what you did — one or more ids, not everything a recall returned.

data.name: type.ReinforceResult
data.value: What a reinforce call recorded.

data.name: type.ReinforceResult.accessedAt
data.value: The instant every named memory's recency clock was set to.

data.name: tool.retain
data.value:
Store something worth remembering — a decision and its reasoning, an error and its fix, a user preference, a durable fact, a question you could not answer. Reach for it the moment you learn something you'd want back later, and write each memory so it stands on its own: a reader months from now, with no other context, should understand it.
STORE THE CLAIM YOU CHECKED, not the claim you would like to be true. Before storing, name what would show you WRONG — and if you cannot name that check, the claim is too vague, so sharpen it until you can. "The DuckDB docs state MERGE is atomic" is a fact you verified by reading them; a bare "MERGE is atomic" is not. Attribution belongs INSIDE the content. An unchecked belief is not a weak fact, it is an OpenQuestion. Set importance by how much it matters, cite what the memory rests on in evidence, put the argument in reasoning, and list any memories it replaces in supersedes (the old ones stay readable, marked superseded; there is no separate supersede call).
ONE MEMORY PER THING THAT CAN DIE ON ITS OWN. "Sergio said the build failed" and "the build failed" are two memories: the saying stays true forever, the claim is superseded the moment you check it yourself. A conclusion and the premises it rests on are ONE — claim in content, derivation in reasoning, because they die together.
YOU DO NOT SUPPLY IDS. The server mints every id and returns them positionally: result[i] is the memory you sent at position i, always, same length, same order. So you cannot cite a memory you are sending in this same call — retain the sources first, then retain the memory that cites them. If that second call fails you are left with valid standalone memories, which is harmless.
RETAIN ALWAYS STORES. It does not merge, block, refuse, or deduplicate. The only write it refuses is a memory already live in exactly this form — same content, same tags, same evidence — which comes back Noop with that memory's id. That is an idempotency guard against a resend, not deduplication: anything less than identical is stored.
DUPLICATES ARE YOUR CALL. Deciding from a similarity score at write time means guessing which tags and which citations you meant to keep, and a memory the server rewrote is one you did not author. Search with recall first when it matters, and correct with supersedes when you find you already knew something.
Set neighbours and each stored memory comes back with that many existing memories nearest it, so "what am I storing next to?" costs no extra round trip. They are reported AFTER the write and change nothing — you owe no answer, and ignoring them loses nothing but a duplicate the curation pass will fold.
Additive: nothing is overwritten or deleted, and a memory you supersede stays readable. Returns one result per memory, in order.

data.name: tool.retain.param.memories
data.value: One or more memories to store — each written to stand on its own.

data.name: tool.retain.param.neighbours
data.value: How many existing memories nearest each stored one to report back. Leave it at 0 and the server does no search at all, which is the cheap path. Ask for a few (2-3) when you want to know what you are storing next to.

data.name: tool.reclaim.param.ids
data.value: The exact memory ids to fetch back.

data.name: tool.recollect.param.options
data.value: The filters and ordering — types (any-of), tags (all-of), limit, sort, direction.

data.name: type.Evidence
data.value:
One cited source. Exactly one arm is set: a memory, a KurrentDB log record, a location in git, or text on the web.
EVIDENCE ANSWERS ONE QUESTION: how can this claim be CHECKED? It does not say how far to trust the memory, and it is NOT an input to ranking — the most rigorous memories carry none, because a check you ran yourself is not a citable source. Its three jobs are AUDIT (a reader confirms the claim without re-deriving it), SUPERSESSION (a successor carries its own citations plus the ones it replaces) and CASCADE (when a cited memory proves wrong, everything resting on it can be found).
Cite only what is OUTSIDE the memory. A check you ran yourself — a search, a build, a test run — is not a source: if it matters, say so in content or reasoning. A search result in particular is not evidence; cite the thing it found, and put "nothing else does this" in reasoning where a reader can discount it.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToMemory
data.value: A citation of another memory. The only arm that makes this memory derived.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToMemory.memory
data.value: The cited memory.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToRecord
data.value: A citation of a KurrentDB log record.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToRecord.record
data.value: The cited KurrentDB log record.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToGit
data.value: A citation of a location in a git repository.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToGit.git
data.value: The cited source location.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToWeb
data.value: A citation of text on the web.

data.name: type.Evidence+ToWeb.web
data.value: The cited page, with the passages that made it worth citing.

data.name: type.GitRef
data.value: A location in a git repository. The ANCHOR is the commit: without it the citation rots silently as the file moves. Prefer a symbol over a line range — a symbol survives a refactor, a line number rots within days. Reach for lines only where there is no symbol to name (an XML element, a config entry, a data file).

data.name: type.GitRef.repo
data.value: owner/name. Leave unset for the repository the memory is being retained from.

data.name: type.GitRef.commit
data.value: The anchor — the revision this citation was true at.

data.name: type.GitRef.branch
data.value: Advisory only: a branch moves, so it anchors nothing.

data.name: type.GitRef.path
data.value: Repo-relative path.

data.name: type.GitRef.symbol
data.value: The type or member cited. Preferred over lines — it survives line drift.

data.name: type.GitRef.lineStart
data.value: Fallback for files with no symbol to name.

data.name: type.GitRef.lineEnd
data.value: Fallback for files with no symbol to name.

data.name: type.GitRef.excerpt
data.value: Optional, 20..1000 characters. Expected when the repo is NOT ours: a third-party repository can go private or vanish, and then the commit resolves to nothing. Our own history is immutable, so an excerpt there is redundant.

data.name: type.WebRef
data.value: A pointer to TEXT on the web — an article, a documentation page, a specification, a post. NOT a file, PDF, archive, or binary target. The ANCHOR is the excerpts, not the URI and not the timestamp: pages are deleted, rewritten, paywalled and moved, and when that happens the excerpt is the only surviving evidence.

data.name: type.WebRef.uri
data.value: The page's address.

data.name: type.WebRef.title
data.value: The page's title, if it has one.

data.name: type.WebRef.excerpts
data.value: Required: 1..5 passages, each 20..1000 characters — the sentences you would quote if asked "where does it say that?". A web citation without one is a bookmark, not a citation, and is rejected. Keep each a passage, not a page: if you need six, you are summarizing the source, and that is a memory of its own.

data.name: type.WebRef.retrievedAt
data.value: When the excerpts were taken — metadata about the excerpt, not the anchor.

data.name: type.LeanMemory
data.value: The lean recall projection: enough to use a memory and judge it, without the provenance trail (evidence, reasoning). For those, request the full body or reclaim by id.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.content
data.value: The memory text.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.importance
data.value: Its salience level.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.memoryId
data.value: Reclaim by this id for the full record.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.memoryType
data.value: What kind of claim this is: truth-apt, a taste, or a question.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.retainedAt
data.value: When the memory was retained — age, for context.

data.name: type.LeanMemory.tags
data.value: Labels carried on the memory.

data.name: type.Memory
data.value: A memory's intrinsic content — the write/command shape passed to retain. The read path returns the folded stored memory; the two shapes are deliberately separate so the write and read models evolve independently.

data.name: type.Memory.content
data.value: The memory's textual content.

data.name: type.Memory.evidence
data.value: The sources this memory cites, in citation order. Evidence answers HOW THIS CAN BE CHECKED — not how far to trust it, and it is NOT an input to ranking. Empty is normal and costs nothing: a check you ran yourself is not a citable source, so the most rigorous memories often cite none at all. If citations lifted a score, a claim copied from a web page would outrank a test you ran.

data.name: type.Memory.reasoning
data.value:
Why this record exists in this shape. Two obligations, in order: (1) why the claim is TRUE — the derivation from the cited sources to the conclusion, present when you synthesized it, absent when it is directly asserted; (2) why it is FILED THIS WAY — only when the type was a judgment call at a contested boundary (Preference vs Fact, when a taste is close to a team standard). Skip (2) when the classification was obvious.
This is also where an INFERENCE lives. A conclusion and the premises it rests on are ONE memory: the claim in content, the derivation here. They die together, so nothing is gained by splitting them. Kept out of content and out of the recall embedding: the embedding indexes the memory's own claim, never the argument for it.

data.name: type.Memory.importance
data.value: The agent's salience rating — how much this memory matters. Higher importance keeps it retrievable longer as recency fades; it does not change the decay rate. Default: Normal.

data.name: type.Memory.supersedes
data.value: Memory ids this memory supersedes (replaces). The superseded ones stay readable, marked superseded. Set at retain — there is no separate supersede operation.

data.name: type.Memory.tags
data.value: Scoped or bare labels.

data.name: type.Memory.type
data.value: What kind of claim this is: truth-apt, a taste, or a question. Not a trust axis — trust is enforced by what you are allowed to WRITE.

data.name: type.Memory.contentTime
data.value: The world-time the content is ABOUT (perceived from the text); a point event sets start == end. NOT the period the claim stays valid — that is derived from this plus the supersession chain. Null when the text implies none.

data.name: type.MemoryImportance
data.value:
The agent's salience rating, set at retain. An additive term in ranking, not a decay control: higher importance keeps a memory's score up as recency fades, so it stays retrievable longer — it does not change the decay rate. A coarse bucket by design.
Values: - Unspecified: Not set — treated as Normal. - Low: Incidental — fine to let it fade. - Normal: The default. - High: Decisions, fixes, preferences worth keeping. - Critical: Top salience — architectural calls, hard-won lessons.

data.name: type.MemoryRef
data.value: A pointer to another memory that supports this one — the id and nothing else. A log position is deliberately absent: the server can look one up from the id whenever it needs it, so a copy here would carry no new information. RecordRef does keep a position, because there you are holding the log record and genuinely know it.

data.name: type.MemoryRef.id
data.value: The cited memory id.

data.name: type.MemoryType
data.value:
What a memory IS. ONE axis only: is this TRUTH-APT, and if not, what is it?
Every other distinction lives in a field that carries it better: a moment vs a standing state is contentTime, an inference is reasoning, what it rests on is evidence, who it applies to is tags, what replaced it is supersedes. THE ADMISSION TEST: if a field already carries the distinction, it is not a type.
There is NO confidence and NO certainty anywhere in this contract. Trust is not a column — it is a rule about what you may WRITE. Store the claim you CHECKED. Name the falsifying check first; if you cannot name what would show you wrong, the claim is too vague. Observing something verifies EXACTLY what you observed: watching a build fail verifies "the build failed", not "the build is broken" and not "the build fails because of X".
Values: - Unspecified: Default / not set. - Fact: An assertion about the world that can be TRUE or FALSE — by far the common case. Scope is irrelevant to the type and so is subject matter: "humans need air", "this project runs tests only via test-runner.cs" and "the build failed at 14:22" are the same KIND of record. Scope is what tags are for; moment-versus-span is what contentTime is for. EVIDENCE IS NOT WHAT MAKES A FACT: most carry none, because a check you ran yourself is not a citable source. Missing evidence costs auditability, never validity and never rank. - Preference: A personal taste that binds its principal ("I prefer tabs"). NOT truth-apt — a taste cannot be false, so asking how far to believe it is a category error. A preference that binds a TEAM is a standard, which is a Fact at that scope. The line is who must follow it. - OpenQuestion: A KNOWN GAP — something unresolved that still needs an answer. Carries no proposition, so it has no truth value and can be neither corroborated nor contradicted. This is also where UNCHECKED BELIEFS go: a working hypothesis is not a low-confidence fact, it is a question with your reading in reasoning. Enumerate them with recollect — that list is your work queue. Terminates by being ANSWERED: retain the answering Fact with supersedes on it. Never citable as evidence — a claim cannot rest on a question.
There is no Observation type (the word named how you came to KNOW something, not the shape of the claim), no Hearsay (that is the write rule's job), no Summary (a consolidation is a Fact citing many memories), no UserProfile (identity is a Fact about a principal), no Procedure (a how-to is a Fact) and no Plan (an intention is a Fact with a future contentTime).

data.name: type.RecallOptions
data.value: The optional knobs for a recall — the query itself is a direct parameter.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.includeFull
data.value: When true, each hit carries the complete folded record instead of the lean projection. Default false: lean hits, easier on your context.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.limit
data.value: How many memories to return after ranking. Ask for a handful (5–10); asking for many more mostly dilutes the top results.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.minScore
data.value: Drop anything the server scores below this cutoff — raise it when you only want strong matches, leave it at 0 to see everything that ranked.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.queryId
data.value: Optional correlation id for this recall; null ⇒ the server assigns one. Keep it to tie later feedback or inspection back to this exact query.

data.name: type.RecallOptions.tags
data.value: Optional pre-filter: only memories carrying these tags are considered. Use it only when you already know the dimension to narrow to; empty ⇒ search everything.

data.name: type.RecallResult
data.value: Result of a recall — hits ranked best-first.

data.name: type.RecallResult.memories
data.value: The recall hits, ranked best-first.

data.name: type.RecallResult.queryId
data.value: Echoes the recall's query id (assigned by the server if it was left empty).

data.name: type.RecalledMemory
data.value: One recall hit — a ranking score plus the memory, lean by default or the full folded record when include-full was set. Exactly one body arm is set.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory+Full
data.value: The complete folded record (as reclaim returns) — present when include-full was set.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory+Full.memory
data.value: The complete folded record of the hit.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory+Lean
data.value: The default lean projection — enough to use and trust a hit.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory+Lean.memory
data.value: The lean projection of the hit.

data.name: type.RecalledMemory.score
data.value: Final ranking score — the alpha-weighted sum of the normalized dimensions; higher = stronger match. A low top score means nothing matched well.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions
data.value: The filters and ordering for a recollect — browse by structure (type/tags), not relevance. Recollect has no payload, so every input lives here.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.direction
data.value: Sort direction. Default: descending.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.limit
data.value: Max memories to return. With a limit, the sort decides which slice you get.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.sort
data.value: How to order results. Default: newest-retained first. Reach for Importance when you want the top-N significant memories rather than the most recent.

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.tags
data.value: Optional filter: only memories carrying ALL of these tags (empty ⇒ no tag filter).

data.name: type.RecollectOptions.types
data.value: Optional filter: any-of these types (empty ⇒ any type).

data.name: type.RecollectSort
data.value:
The dimension a recollect orders its results by (there is no relevance here — that's recall).
Values: - Unspecified: Not set — defaults to RetainedAt. - RetainedAt: When the memory was recorded — chronological. The default. - LastAccessedAt: The recency clock — surfaces what has been salient (recalled) lately. - Importance: The agent's salience rating — surfaces the significant ones. Pairs well with a limit: the top-N important memories rather than arbitrary ones.

data.name: type.RecordRef
data.value: A pointer to a KurrentDB log record that supports this memory.

data.name: type.RecordRef.id
data.value: The record's id.

data.name: type.RecordRef.position
data.value: Its position in the log (exact, replayable).

data.name: type.Neighbour
data.value: An existing memory near one you just stored. Advisory — it was reported after the write and you owe no answer.

data.name: type.Neighbour.memory
data.value: The neighbouring memory itself.

data.name: type.Neighbour.distance
data.value: Vector distance, SMALLER = more alike. Comparable across queries, unlike a blended search score.

data.name: type.Neighbour.keywordMatch
data.value: The keyword search matched this memory too. A keyword match at a low distance is a restatement in mostly the same words; a low distance alone is a reword.

data.name: type.RetainOutcome
data.value:
What retain did with one memory.
Values: - Unspecified: Not set. - Created: The memory was stored. - Noop: A live memory is already byte-for-byte this one — same content, same tags, same evidence — so nothing was written and memoryId is that memory.

data.name: type.RetainResult
data.value: Result of a retain — one outcome per input memory, in the same order.

data.name: type.RetainResult.results
data.value: One result per input memory, in order.

data.name: type.RetainedMemory
data.value: The outcome for a single stored memory.

data.name: type.RetainedMemory.outcome
data.value: What the server did with this memory: Created or Noop.

data.name: type.RetainedMemory.memoryId
data.value: The newly written memory for Created; the existing, untouched one for Noop.

data.name: type.RetainedMemory.neighbours
data.value: The live memories nearest this one, nearest first — present only when you asked for them. Advisory: reported after the write, nothing was blocked or changed, and you owe no answer.

data.name: type.SortDirection
data.value:
Sort direction for a recollect listing.
Values: - Unspecified: Not set — defaults to Descending. - Descending: High → low: newest / most-important / most-recently-accessed first. - Ascending: Low → high: oldest / least first.

data.name: type.StoredMemory
data.value: The complete, folded read model of a single memory — every lifecycle event applied. Self-contained, for inspection and direct fetch (reclaim/recollect), not for ranked retrieval. Deliberately separate from the memory command shape so read and write models evolve independently.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.content
data.value: The memory's textual content.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.reasoning
data.value: Why the claim is true and, when it was a judgment call, why it is filed this way.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.evidence
data.value: What this memory rests on — the cited sources. Answers how the claim can be CHECKED; empty is normal.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.importance
data.value: The salience level set at retain (higher keeps it retrievable longer as recency fades).

data.name: type.StoredMemory.lastAccessedAt
data.value: When the memory was last accessed — the recency clock, advanced by each recall. Null if never accessed.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.memoryId
data.value: Unique identifier of the memory.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.memoryType
data.value: What kind of claim this is: truth-apt, a taste, or a question.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.retainedAt
data.value: When the memory was retained.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.supersededAt
data.value: When a newer memory superseded this one, if any.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.supersededBy
data.value: The memory that superseded this one; set only when superseded-at is set.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.supersedes
data.value: Memory ids this memory supersedes (replaces).

data.name: type.StoredMemory.tags
data.value: Scoped or bare labels.

data.name: type.StoredMemory.contentTime
data.value: The world-time the content is ABOUT (perceived from the text). Validity is derived from this plus the supersession chain.

data.name: type.Tag
data.value: An agent-agnostic filter label with an optional scope (namespace). Scoped tags let you filter on a typed dimension (e.g. project:kurrentdb) without a contract change per dimension, and the same scope can repeat on one memory. Both value and scope are sanitized to lower kebab-case, so tags are canonical.

data.name: type.Tag.scope
data.value: Optional namespace — lower kebab-case; empty ⇒ bare tag.

data.name: type.Tag.value
data.value: The label — lower kebab-case.

data.name: type.TemporalContext
data.value:
The world-time the memory's content is ABOUT, as perceived from its text (may be fuzzy). This is CONTENT time, distinct from the storage clocks (retained-at, last-accessed-at). A point-in-time event sets the end equal to the start; a null end means ongoing.
It is NOT the period the claim stays valid, and the two come apart: "the build failed at 14:22" is ABOUT a moment in the past and is valid FOREVER. VALIDITY IS DERIVED, never stored — it runs from this memory's start to its successor's start, or stays open when nothing superseded it. Storing an end would fabricate a guess about the future.
Whether a claim can lapse falls out of the shape: closed and entirely past means SETTLED and can never lapse; open-ended asserts the present and can; closed in the future can (a scheduled deploy can be cancelled).

data.name: type.TemporalContext.from
data.value: Start of the state, or the moment of a point event.

data.name: type.TemporalContext.to
data.value: End of the interval; null ⇒ ongoing / open-ended.

data.name: tool.search
data.value: Search the database's LOG RECORDS by meaning — not recall (that searches your own memories, which are claims you wrote). Records are the events themselves, so reach for this when you need the evidence rather than the conclusion: what a stream actually contains, when something happened, which payload carried a value, whether an event of some shape was ever written. Matching runs over a flattened projection of the payload, so field names and values both count. Narrow with the filters whenever you can, schemaName first — "every OrderCancelled" is the question people actually ask of a log. Filtering is free and never costs you part of the page: the engine applies it while selecting candidates, so a scoped search returns a full limit drawn from the matching records even when they are a handful among millions. Pick one per group: stream or category, and one of schemaName / schemaId / schemaFormat. Only JSON records are indexed: a non-JSON or empty payload cannot be found here. Read-only and side-effect-free — unlike recall, it records no access.

data.name: tool.query
data.value:
Read the database's log with SQL — not search (that ranks by meaning), this one filters, groups and counts EXACTLY. Reach for it when the question has a precise answer ranking cannot give: how many, since when, which streams, grouped by what. One table is visible, kdb.records, holding every record the database has; naming any other table is rejected, and so are table functions.
Columns: record_id, log_position, stream, stream_revision, category, schema_name, schema_id, schema_format, created_at (epoch ms), expires_at, deleted, data, metadata.
data holds the payload, and JSON records carry their JSON verbatim — so json_extract_string(data, '$.orderId') works directly. Non-JSON payloads arrive base64 encoded, so filter on schema_format = 'Json' before touching data. Ask for the columns you want: SELECT * pulls every payload in the result into your context. Read-only.

data.name: tool.query.param.sql
data.value: A DuckDB SELECT over kdb.records, e.g. "SELECT stream, count(*) AS n FROM kdb.records WHERE schema_name = 'OrderCancelled' GROUP BY stream ORDER BY n DESC".

data.name: tool.query.param.limit
data.value: Max rows to return, capped by the server. 0 ⇒ server default. Prefer aggregating in SQL over pulling rows back and counting them yourself.

data.name: type.QueryResult
data.value: The rows one query returned.

data.name: type.QueryResult.rows
data.value: One object per row, keyed by the column names your SELECT produced.

data.name: type.QueryResult.truncated
data.value: True when the row cap cut the result short — the answer is INCOMPLETE, so narrow the query or aggregate in SQL rather than trusting what came back.

data.name: tool.search.param.query
data.value: What you are looking for, in natural language — describe the event ("a payment failed with an expired card"), not keywords.

data.name: tool.search.param.options
data.value: Optional knobs — limit, minimum score, and the scope/schema filters. Null ⇒ server defaults, searching the whole log.

data.name: type.SearchOptions
data.value: Optional knobs for a records search. Two groups are ALTERNATIVES, not combinations: stream/category, and schemaName/schemaId/schemaFormat. Setting more than one of a group is rejected.

data.name: type.SearchOptions.limit
data.value: How many records to return. A handful (5–10) is usually right; a filter never costs you part of the page, so there is no need to oversample. 0 ⇒ server default.

data.name: type.SearchOptions.schemaName
data.value: Only records of this type ("OrderCancelled", "CustomerRegistered"), across every version of it. The sharpest filter the log has, and usually the one you want. Alternative to schemaId and schemaFormat.

data.name: type.SearchOptions.minScore
data.value: Drop anything scored below this cutoff. Raise it when you only want strong matches; 0 ⇒ everything that ranked.

data.name: type.SearchOptions.stream
data.value: Look only in this stream, named exactly ("order-8fc1a2"). Alternative to category.

data.name: type.SearchOptions.category
data.value: Look only in streams sharing this prefix — the text before the first '-' in the stream name ("order" covers "order-8fc1a2" and "order-3b90ff"). Alternative to stream, because a category IS a set of streams.

data.name: type.SearchOptions.schemaId
data.value: Only records written against this exact registered schema version. Alternative to schemaName and schemaFormat, both of which it already implies.

data.name: type.SearchOptions.schemaFormat
data.value: Only records in this payload encoding, as the record carries it ("Json"). The coarsest of the three; alternative to schemaName and schemaId.

data.name: type.SearchResult
data.value: The hits for one search, ranked best-first.

data.name: type.SearchResult.hits
data.value: The matching records, strongest first.

data.name: type.RecordHit
data.value: One search hit: the record and how strongly it matched.

data.name: type.RecordHit.score
data.value: Blended relevance across the meaning and keyword legs; higher = stronger. Your weak-match signal: a low top score means nothing matched well.

data.name: type.RecordHit.record
data.value: The record as the index holds it, payload included.

data.name: type.Record
data.value: One record the database wrote, as the index holds it.

data.name: type.Record.recordId
data.value: The record's unique identifier.

data.name: type.Record.stream
data.value: The stream the record belongs to.

data.name: type.Record.category
data.value: The set of streams this one belongs to: the text before the first '-' in the stream name.

data.name: type.Record.logPosition
data.value: The record's position in the global log — a stable cursor, since the log only grows.

data.name: type.Record.schema
data.value: What shape the payload is in.

data.name: type.Record.properties
data.value: The properties the record carries — user-defined keys, and system keys prefixed with "$" ($correlationId, $causationId). Present exactly as written.

data.name: type.Record.data
data.value: The record payload, as written.

data.name: type.Record.createdAt
data.value: When the record was written.

data.name: type.SchemaInfo
data.value: What the record's payload conforms to.

data.name: type.SchemaInfo.format
data.value: Payload encoding, as the indexer read it off the record ("Json").

data.name: type.SchemaInfo.name
data.value: The record type ("order-placed", "customer-registered").

data.name: type.SchemaInfo.id
data.value: The registered schema version the record conforms to; empty when the record carried no schema id.
